Dried
DRYDE
v. (past, pp.)
From dry, Old English drygan. Webster 1828: freed from moisture; exsiccated. In the Authorized Version the word marks the great acts of God over water — the flood receding, the Red sea, the Jordan — and also the failing of a brook that taught a prophet to trust the God who dried it.

Biblical Definition

Dried in Scripture is usually God acting on water. After the flood the raven went to and fro until the waters were dried up from off the earth (Genesis 8:7), and in due time was the earth dried (Genesis 8:14). At the Jordan Joshua tells the nation why the stones were set up: the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you, until ye were passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red sea, which he dried up from before us (Joshua 4:23). Two generations, two waters, one God who dries a path for His people. The word also marks judgment and testing. Israel in the wilderness complains, our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes (Numbers 11:6) — contempt for daily bread. Samson’s green withs were never dried (Judges 16:7), the first of his careless bargains with his own strength. And Elijah, fed by ravens at Cherith, learns the harder lesson: it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land (1 Kings 17:7) — the same drought he had announced, reaching him, and sending him on to the widow of Zarephath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DRIED as freed from moisture or made dry; exsiccated. The KJV uses it above all of waters God removes to make a way, and of streams He allows to fail.

expand to see more

DRIED, pp. of DRY — Freed from moisture or sap; exsiccated.

DRY, v.t. — To free from water or moisture; to exsiccate; to drain.

DRY, a. — Destitute of moisture; free from water or wetness; arid; not moist.

The passive participle in Scripture almost always has God as its agent, whether stated or implied. The waters do not simply recede; they are dried up from before a people who are being brought over.

Key Scripture

Genesis 8:7 — "And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth."

Genesis 8:14 — "And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, was the earth dried."

Numbers 11:6 — "But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes."

Joshua 4:23 — "For the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you, until ye were passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red sea, which he dried up from before us, until we were gone over:"

1 Kings 17:7 — "And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is Numbers 11:6 — a people whose souls are dried away in the presence of daily provision, because the provision is not the kind they wanted.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and nothing is being contested. What repays attention is the pairing of Joshua 4:23 with Numbers 11:6, since the same generation is in view. God dried the Red sea and later the Jordan — both times to bring a people over, both times commemorated with a memorial and a catechism for children — and the same people said our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes. Manna was bread from heaven, given daily, sufficient, and free, and it was despised because it was ordinary. The parallel to a church that finds the ordinary means of grace insufficiently interesting is exact.

The principle to recover is that God dries streams as well as seas, and both are His work. Elijah had just announced a drought at the word of the LORD and was then sustained beside a brook that the drought itself would kill. When it failed, he was not abandoned but redirected — to a widow in Zidon, to a handful of meal, to a resurrection. The dried brook was the means of the next thing. This is providence at its most uncomfortable and most instructive: the believer is not promised that the stream he was drinking from will not fail, but that the God who dried the Red sea has a reason and a next place.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew verb is charab or yabesh, both meaning to be dry or waste; yabbashah, the noun, is the dry land of Genesis 1:9 and of the sea crossings.

expand to see more

Hebrew charab (H2717) — to be dry, waste, desolate; the waters were dried up from off the earth (Genesis 8:7).

Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to be dry, to wither; the earth dried (Genesis 8:14) and the brook dried up (1 Kings 17:7).

Hebrew yabbashah (H3004) — dry land; the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9) and the ground Israel walked at the sea and the Jordan.

Hebrew yabesh in Numbers 11:6 — our soul is dried away, the same withering verb turned inward on the appetite.

Greek xeraino (G3583) — to dry up, wither; the water thereof was dried up (Revelation 16:12), the last of the Bible’s dried waters.

Usage

"The LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you (Joshua 4:23) — the second drying, taught to children beside twelve stones."

"Our soul is dried away… beside this manna (Numbers 11:6) — daily bread despised for being ordinary."

"The brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land (1 Kings 17:7) — the failing stream as the means of the next provision."
